name: Security Assessment and Testing
plainMeaning: This domain is about proving that security really works. You plan tests and audits, carry them out, collect the results, report them to the right people and make sure problems get fixed.

topics.name: Assessment, test and audit strategies
topics.simpleExplanation: Think of a school that wants to know if its safety rules really work. It must decide what to check, who will check it, where, and how often. Its own staff can check some things. An outside expert can check others. A government inspector may also come. Security works the same way. A company writes a plan for checking its safeguards. The plan must match the company's goals, risks and laws. It must also fit where the systems live, such as an office, a cloud or both.

studyNotes.heading: Why an organization needs a strategy
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we will look at why an organization needs a written plan for checking its security, and what that plan must contain.

A control is a safeguard that reduces risk. A door lock is a control, and so is a rule that two people must approve a large payment. A strategy is the written plan for checking that those controls really work.

Think about your home. You could test the smoke alarm whenever you happen to remember. Or you could decide that on the first Sunday of each month, one named person tests it and writes down the result. The second way is a strategy. It is planned, it has an owner, and it leaves a record.

A good strategy answers five plain questions. Why are we checking? The reason may be a law, a contract or a known risk. What is in scope? Scope means what is included and what is left out. Who will do the work, and who will read the results and act on them? Where do the systems live? And when, and how often, will the checks happen?

Now think like a manager. A strategy starts from business goals, risk and legal duties. It does not start from a favorite tool. Senior management must support it, because testing costs money and can disturb the business. Without that support, findings are ignored.

The exam outline uses the word validate. To design a strategy is to write it. To validate a strategy is to confirm that the strategy itself is still right. Do the tests still match the risks? Are the results reaching people who can act? Are problems really being fixed? Review the strategy on a regular schedule, and also whenever the business changes.

Here is a workplace example. A retail company buys a smaller online firm. The old plan says nothing about the new firm's systems, its customers or the laws of the country where it trades. The plan was fine last year, but it is no longer valid, so it must be updated before more tests are run.

Here is your takeaway. A strategy begins with business goals, risk and law, and it must be checked again whenever the business changes.

studyNotes.heading: Test, assessment and audit
studyNotes.body:
Next, we will separate three words that sound alike but mean different things: test, assessment and audit. The exam expects you to know which one a scenario describes.

A test checks one control and gives a clear result. Does the door lock when it closes? Yes or no.

An assessment is a wider review of a system or a whole program. It often includes several tests, and it ends with advice on how to improve.

An audit is a formal check against a fixed standard. It is based on evidence, and it is done by someone independent of the work. Evidence is the proof that supports a conclusion.

Let us use a car as an everyday picture. You press the brake pedal in the driveway to see whether the brakes work. That is a test. A mechanic spends an hour looking over the whole car and tells you what to repair soon. That is an assessment. A government inspector checks the car against the published road safety rules, records the proof and issues a pass or a fail. That is an audit.

A simple way to hold on to this is to remember three questions. A test asks: does it work? An assessment asks: how good are we? An audit asks: can you prove that you meet the standard?

Now a workplace example. A hospital tries to log in with a disabled account, to see whether access is really blocked. That is a test. It then asks a consultant to review its whole access program and recommend improvements. That is an assessment. Finally, an independent auditor checks its access records against a health privacy standard. That is an audit.

Assessors commonly use three methods, and these are worth knowing as a set. To examine is to read documents and records. To interview is to talk to the people who do the work. To test is to try the control and see what happens. Testing usually gives the strongest proof, because it shows what really happens and not what people say happens.

Here is what to take away. A test checks one thing, an assessment judges and advises, and an audit proves compliance with a standard through independent evidence.

studyNotes.heading: Internal, external and third-party work
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at who does the checking, because that decides how far the results can be trusted.

The exam outline gives three groups, and each comes with a short description.

- Internal: within your organization's control. Your own staff usually do the work.
- External: outside your organization's control. Typically, an outside firm does the work.
- Third-party: outside your enterprise's control. Another party, such as a regulator or a major customer, carries out or requires the check. A third-party review can also mean an independent check of a vendor.

Think about a restaurant. The owner walks around the kitchen every morning, checking that it is clean. That is internal. The owner pays a private food safety consultant to visit twice a year. That is external. A health inspector arrives on behalf of the local government, and the owner did not choose the inspector or the day. That is third-party.

Each has strengths. Internal work is cheaper and can happen often. Your staff know the systems well. But they are less independent, and they may find it difficult to criticize their colleagues. External work is more independent, and others trust it more, but it costs more and the outsiders take time to learn your systems. Third-party work carries the most weight with others, but you have the least control over its timing and its focus.

Books use these words in slightly different ways. Some call a hired firm a third party. So do not rely on the label alone. Read the scenario and ask two questions. Who ordered the work? And who is doing it?

Most organizations use all three. Here is a workplace example. A bank's own team runs weekly vulnerability scans, which are automated searches for known weaknesses. A hired firm carries out a penetration test, which is an approved attempt to break in, once a year. And the banking regulator inspects the bank on its own schedule.

The manager's question is always the same. Who needs to trust this result? If it is only your own team, internal work may be enough. If it is a board, a customer or a regulator, you need more independence.

Here is your takeaway. Independence and cost generally rise as you move from internal, to external, to third-party.

studyNotes.heading: Location: on-premises, cloud and hybrid
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at where the systems live, because location changes what you are allowed to test and how you get your evidence.

On-premises means the systems are in your own building. You control the hardware, the network and the doors. You can test almost everything, and you can walk an auditor through the server room.

Cloud means a provider runs the systems in its own data centers, and you reach them over a network. Responsibility is shared, which means that the security duties are split between the provider and the customer. The split depends on the service.

- Infrastructure as a Service, or IaaS: you rent servers. You check the operating system, the applications and the data.
- Platform as a Service, or PaaS: you rent a place to run your own code. You check your application and your data.
- Software as a Service, or SaaS: you rent a finished application. You mainly check your users, your settings and your data.

Think about housing. If you own a house, you can inspect every pipe. If you rent a bare apartment, the landlord looks after the building, and you are responsible for what you bring in. If you stay in a furnished hotel room, nearly everything is done for you, but you must still lock your door and look after your passport.

In every model, the customer remains responsible for its own data and for who can reach it.

You usually cannot visit a cloud data center, or test it freely. So before any test, read the provider's testing rules and your contract. Testing without checking may break the contract, and it may even be illegal. For the parts that you cannot test, you rely on the provider's independent audit reports.

Hybrid mixes the two. Check each side, and also check the connection between them, because that link is easily forgotten. Think of a customer website in the cloud that reads from a database in your own building. Each side can look secure while the link between them is weak.

Location also affects law. Data held in another country may fall under that country's rules, so ask where your data is stored.

Here is what to take away. Where the system lives decides what you may test, whose rules apply and what evidence you can collect.

studyNotes.heading: Vendor considerations
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at how you check a vendor, which is a company that supplies a service to you. More and more of an organization's systems are run by someone else, so this matters a great deal.

Think about hiring a builder. You could simply trust the builder's smile. You could ask for references. You could write into the agreement that you may inspect the work. Or you could ask to see the certificate from the building inspector. Each one gives you more confidence than the last.

With vendors, there are four main tools.

A security questionnaire is a list of written questions that the vendor answers. It is useful for a first look, but it is weak on its own, because the vendor is simply marking its own work.

A service level agreement, or SLA, is the promised level of service, in writing, such as how much of the time the service must be available.

A right-to-audit clause is a term in the contract that lets you check the vendor. It must be agreed before the contract is signed. It is very hard to add later, once the vendor already has your business.

An independent audit report is an outside auditor's findings about the vendor's controls. This is often the most practical strong evidence, particularly with very large providers that will not let individual customers visit.

Also ask about the vendor's own suppliers, because your data may travel further than you expect. A supplier's supplier is sometimes called a fourth party.

Here is a workplace example. A company is choosing a provider to handle its staff payroll records. First, it sends a questionnaire to narrow down the choice. Next, it reads the independent audit reports of the two best candidates. Then it adds a right-to-audit clause and a duty to report breaches quickly to the contract. Finally, it reviews the vendor every year, because a safe vendor can become an unsafe one.

Now remember the most important rule of this part. You can hand over the work, but you cannot hand over the accountability. If the vendor loses your customers' data, your customers and your regulator will still look to you.

Here is your takeaway. Build your right to check into the contract, prefer independent evidence, and stay accountable.

studyNotes.heading: Putting the strategy together
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will build one strategy from beginning to end, so you can see how all these pieces fit.

Think about planning the health checks for a family. Everyone gets a basic check every year. A person with a heart condition is seen more often, and by a specialist. The frequency follows the risk. Security testing works the same way.

Now here is a workplace example. A mid-sized online shop takes card payments, keeps its website in the cloud and runs its warehouse system in its own building. Let us walk through the steps.

First, the shop lists its goals and duties. It must keep selling online, and it must follow the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, or PCI DSS, which protects card data.

Second, it ranks its systems by risk. The payment system comes first, then the website, and then the warehouse system.

Third, it chooses who does what. Its own staff run scans and review logs, which are records of events. PCI DSS requires external vulnerability scans at least once every three months, carried out by an approved scanning company. It also requires penetration testing at least once every twelve months, and after any significant change. So an outside firm is booked. And each year an independent assessor checks compliance with the standard.

Fourth, it handles location. On the cloud side, it reads the provider's testing rules. For the warehouse, it can test directly. It also tests the link between the two.

Fifth, it agrees who receives the results and how fast problems must be fixed.

Sixth, it obtains senior management's approval and funding.

Finally, it validates the plan each year. Are findings being closed? Did a real incident reveal something the tests missed? If an attack succeeded through a system that was never in scope, the strategy itself has failed, and it must change.

On the exam, watch for answers that jump straight to buying a tool or running a test. If nobody has decided what the business needs, that is the wrong place to start. The best first step is usually to understand the goals, the risks, the scope and the requirements.

Here is what to take away. Test more often where the risk is higher, choose independence to match who must trust the result, and keep checking that the plan itself is right.

A wide review of a system or program that often includes tests and ends with advice.
A formal, independent, evidence-based check against a fixed standard.
Work done by your own staff, within your organization's control.
Work outside your organization's control, usually done by a firm from outside.
Work outside your enterprise's control, such as a check by a regulator or customer, or an independent check of a vendor.
A setup that uses both your own site and the cloud.
A contract term that lets a customer check how a vendor protects its data.
The split of security duties between a cloud provider and its customer.

keyPoints: A strategy starts from business goals, risk and legal duties.
Audits are formal, independent and based on evidence.

topics.memoryHook: Why, What, Who, Where, When: answer these five and you have a strategy.

question.prompt: A hospital is moving its patient booking system to a Software as a Service provider. The contract does not allow customers to test the provider's platform. The hospital still needs confidence in the security of the service. What should the security manager do?
options: Run an unannounced penetration test so that the provider has no time to prepare for it
Accept the security statement on the provider's website and record the matter as closed
Review the provider's independent audit report and check the hospital's own settings
Remove the system from the plan because the provider now carries all of the accountability
question.explanation: An independent report gives trusted evidence without breaking the contract, and the hospital still checks the part it controls. An unannounced test is tempting, but it breaks the contract and may be illegal. The hospital also stays accountable for its patients' data.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's internal security team tests the company's controls every month. The board now wants greater assurance that it can show to its shareholders. What would BEST add independence?
options: Asking the internal team to carry out the same tests weekly instead of monthly
An audit by a firm from outside the company
Having the internal team's own manager sign every set of test results
Buying a more advanced scanning tool for the internal team to run each month
practiceQuestions.explanation: An outside firm has no stake in the results, so others trust its findings more. Testing more often is tempting, but the same people are still checking their own organization, so independence does not improve.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A manufacturer has just merged with a company in another country. Its assessment and audit strategy was approved eight months ago and has not been changed. What should the security manager do FIRST?
options: Continue with the current plan until the next scheduled yearly review date
Run a penetration test against every system owned by the merged company
Ask the other company's security team to keep following its own separate plan
Review the strategy against the new risks, scope and legal duties
practiceQuestions.explanation: A major business change is a reason to validate the strategy, because its scope and legal duties have changed. Testing everything is tempting, but testing without a sound plan and approval is the wrong first step.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company rents virtual servers from a provider under an Infrastructure as a Service agreement. Which items are the company's responsibility to check?
options: Its operating systems, applications and data
The physical locks and guards at each of the provider's data centers
The layer of provider software that runs beneath every customer's servers
The electricity and cooling systems inside the provider's own buildings
practiceQuestions.explanation: With Infrastructure as a Service, the customer manages everything from the operating system upward. The physical locks and guards are tempting because they matter, but they are the provider's duty.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security team wants to run a penetration test, meaning an approved attempt to break in, against an application hosted with a large cloud provider. What should the team do FIRST?
options: Begin at night, when the provider has fewer staff watching its systems
Ask the application's developers to list any weaknesses they already know about
Check the provider's testing rules and the terms of the contract
Run the test at a low speed so that the provider's monitoring does not notice it
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cloud testing is governed by the provider's rules and the contract, and ignoring them can be a breach or a crime. Asking developers is useful, but it does not establish whether the test is allowed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's customer website is in the cloud and reads from a database in the company's own building. An audit team tested the cloud side and the on-premises side and found both sound. What is the MOST important area still to check?
options: The physical condition of the building's main reception area
The connection between the two environments
The colors and page layout used throughout the customer website
The age of the laptop computers issued to the company's sales staff
practiceQuestions.explanation: In a hybrid setup, the link between the two sides is part of the system and is easily forgotten. Each side can be sound while the connection between them is weak.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A payment network requires a formal, evidence-based check, by someone independent, that a merchant meets a published standard. Which activity does this describe?
options: Audit
Vulnerability scan
Security assessment
Tabletop exercise
practiceQuestions.explanation: An audit is formal, independent, based on evidence and measured against a fixed standard. An assessment is tempting, but it is a wider review that ends with advice for improvement.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company is negotiating a contract with a delivery firm that will store customer addresses. The company wants to be able to verify the firm's security during the contract. What is the BEST step?
options: Ask the firm to send a friendly email each year confirming that all is well
Rely on the firm's strong reputation among other companies in its market
Request that the firm's website display a clear statement about security
Add a right-to-audit clause
practiceQuestions.explanation: A right-to-audit clause creates an enforceable right to check the vendor, and it must be agreed before signing. Reputation is tempting, but it is not evidence and it gives the company no rights.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An outsourced customer service firm loses a company's customer records because of its own weak controls. The contract places operational security duties on the firm. Who remains accountable to the customers for protecting their data?
options: The firm's systems administrator who made the configuration error
The outsourcing firm alone, because it agreed to do the security work
The company that entrusted the data to the firm
The insurance company that provides cover for the outsourcing firm
practiceQuestions.explanation: Work can be outsourced, but accountability cannot. The contract may allow the company to recover its costs from the firm, which makes the second option tempting, but the company still answers to its customers.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company stores customer records with a cloud provider that keeps copies in several countries. When scoping a compliance review, what is the MOST important question to ask about location?
options: Which provider data center has the newest computer hardware
Which laws apply in the countries where the data is held
Which time zone suits the provider's customer support staff
Which country offers the provider the lowest electricity prices
practiceQuestions.explanation: Data held in another country may fall under that country's laws, so the review must take this into account. The other options concern cost or convenience and do not affect legal duties.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has 200 systems and a limited testing budget. It cannot test every system equally often. How should the security manager set the testing frequency?
options: Test more often where business risk is higher
Divide the budget into 200 equal parts, one for each of the systems
Test each system in alphabetical order until the money has run out
Test only the newest systems, because they have had the least testing so far
practiceQuestions.explanation: A strategy follows risk, so the most important and most exposed systems are tested more often. Equal shares are tempting because they seem fair, but they spend too little on the systems that matter most.

topics.name: Vulnerability assessment and penetration testing
topics.simpleExplanation: Imagine checking your house for safety. Walking around and noting every open window is a vulnerability assessment. A vulnerability is a weakness. Hiring someone to actually climb through the window is a penetration test. It proves how far a burglar could get. Both need clear permission first. Companies use tools to find weaknesses and a standard score to rank them. They also use teams. One team attacks, one team defends, and sometimes they work together and learn from each other.

studyNotes.heading: Vulnerability assessment
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we will look at what a vulnerability assessment is, and the different kinds of scan it uses.

A vulnerability is a weakness that could be used to cause harm. A vulnerability assessment finds and lists weaknesses. It does not use them to break in.

Think about walking around your house at night. You check every window and every door, and you write down which ones are unlocked. You do not climb in. That is a vulnerability assessment.

Assessments mostly rely on scans, which are automated checks run by software. There are four common kinds, and you should know them as a set.

- Network discovery scan: finds which devices exist and which ports are open. A port is a numbered door into a computer, through which a service is offered.
- Network vulnerability scan: looks for known weaknesses on those devices.
- Web application scan: looks for flaws in websites, such as poor handling of what users type.
- Database scan: looks for flaws in databases, such as weak settings and default accounts.

A discovery scan may report each port as open, closed or filtered. Open means a service is answering. Closed means nothing is listening. Filtered means something, usually a firewall, is blocking the scanner, so it cannot tell. A firewall is a device or program that filters network traffic.

Discovery scans use a few different techniques. One well-known technique is the SYN scan, sometimes called a half-open scan. SYN is short for synchronize. It is the first message in the three-step greeting that starts a network connection. The scanner sends that first message, sees the reply and never finishes the greeting.

Here is a workplace example. A hospital runs a discovery scan and finds a medical device on the network that nobody had listed. A vulnerability scan then shows that it has a well-known weakness. Nobody broke in, but the hospital now knows something important. It cannot protect what it does not know about.

Scanning is not a one-time event. New flaws are announced every day, so a clean result last month tells you little about today. Scans should run regularly, and after any significant change.

Here is your takeaway. A vulnerability assessment finds and lists weaknesses without using them, and it should be repeated regularly.

studyNotes.heading: Scan accuracy and credentialed scans
studyNotes.body:
Next, we will look at how far you can trust a scan, and at one simple change that makes scans far more accurate.

Tools make two kinds of mistake. A false positive reports a problem that is not real. A false negative misses a problem that is real.

Think about a smoke alarm. If it goes off when you make toast, that is a false positive. It is annoying, and it wastes your time. If it stays silent during a real fire, that is a false negative. That one can kill you. In security, too, the false negative is the more dangerous, because nobody knows there is anything to fix. It is why a clean scan never proves that a system is safe.

False positives still do harm. If staff chase hundreds of false alarms, they lose trust in the tool. That is why people must confirm results before reporting them.

Now, there are two ways to scan. An uncredentialed scan has no login. It shows what an outsider would see from the network. A credentialed scan, also called an authenticated scan, gives the scanner a login. It can then look inside the system and see the installed software, the settings and any missing patches. A patch is a software fix.

Picture a doctor. An uncredentialed scan is a doctor who looks at you from across the room. A credentialed scan is a doctor who gets to examine you properly.

A credentialed scan gives more accurate results, with fewer false positives and fewer false negatives. But it brings its own risk. That login is valuable, so give it only the rights it needs, store it safely and watch how it is used.

Here is a workplace example. An uncredentialed scan of 50 servers finds only a few issues, and the team feels pleased. A credentialed scan of the same servers then finds that 30 of them are missing important patches. The first scan was not wrong about what an outsider sees. It simply could not see inside.

On the exam, when a scenario asks for the most accurate or complete picture of missing patches, think of a credentialed scan.

Here is what to take away. A false negative is the more dangerous error, and a credentialed scan sees more because it logs in.

studyNotes.heading: CVE and CVSS
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at two terms that are very often confused: CVE and CVSS. One names a flaw, and the other scores it.

Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVE, is a public list of known flaws. Each flaw gets a unique name, made of the letters CVE, a year and a number. CVE-2014-0160 is one example. CVE does not tell you how bad a flaw is. It only gives everyone the same name for the same flaw.

The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, or CVSS, rates the severity of a flaw from 0.0 to 10.0. It is maintained by a global group called the Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams.

Think about a car recall. The recall number identifies exactly which fault is meant. That is like CVE. A separate rating says whether the fault is a minor rattle or whether the brakes may fail. That is like CVSS.

These are the score bands, and you must know them exactly.

- None: 0.0
- Low: 0.1 to 3.9
- Medium: 4.0 to 6.9
- High: 7.0 to 8.9
- Critical: 9.0 to 10.0

Let us work through some examples. A score of 3.9 is Low, but 4.0 is Medium. A score of 6.9 is Medium, but 7.0 is High. A score of 8.9 is High, but 9.0 is Critical.

CVSS is built from groups of measures. In version 3.1 they are base, temporal and environmental. The base group describes the flaw itself. Temporal covers things that change over time. Environmental adjusts the score for your own organization. Version 4.0 renames temporal to threat, and adds a supplemental group.

The base score is general, and it knows nothing about your business. Here is a workplace example. A flaw that scores 8.0 is on your public payment system. A flaw that scores 9.2 is on a spare test computer with no real data. A flaw's score matters, but so do its exposure and the value of what it affects. A manager may rightly fix the 8.0 first.

Here is your takeaway. CVE names the flaw and CVSS scores it. Know the bands exactly, and then let business risk set the order of repair.

studyNotes.heading: Penetration testing phases
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at penetration testing, and the order in which it happens. The order is something the exam can test directly.

A penetration test goes further than a scan. A tester, with permission, tries to use weaknesses to break in. To use a weakness in this way is to exploit it. The point is to prove the real impact.

Going back to our house, a scan notes the open window. A penetration test climbs through it, and finds out whether the burglar could reach the safe.

A United States government body, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, or NIST, publishes a guide called Special Publication 800-115. It gives four phases, in this order.

- Planning: agree the goals and the limits, and get written approval.
- Discovery: gather information about the target and scan for weaknesses.
- Attack: try to exploit the weaknesses and break in.
- Reporting: record the findings and give advice.

Two details make these phases less simple than they look. First, the attack phase feeds back into discovery. When a tester gets into one machine, the tester often sees new systems from there, so the tester goes back to discovery and looks again. Second, reporting is not only the end. It happens alongside the other phases, as the tester writes things down, and it finishes with the final report.

Some books use five steps instead: planning, information gathering and discovery, vulnerability scanning, exploitation, and reporting. These are the same ideas divided differently. Whichever list a question uses, planning and approval come first, and reporting finishes the job.

Here is a worked example. A company hires a tester to check its online shop. In planning, the two sides agree that only the shop is in scope, and a senior manager signs the approval. In discovery, the tester finds a forgotten test page. In attack, the tester uses that page to reach a staff system. From there, the tester spots a database that had not been visible, and so returns to discovery. Finally, the report explains what happened, how serious it is and how to fix the cause.

A penetration test is a sample in time. It shows what one tester found in those days. It does not prove that nothing else exists.

Here is what to take away. The four phases are planning, discovery, attack and reporting, and attack can lead back to discovery.

studyNotes.heading: Rules of engagement and box types
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at the limits of a test, and at how much the tester is told before starting.

Rules of engagement are the written limits of the test. Senior management must approve them. Without permission, a penetration test is a crime. A spoken yes from one department head is not enough.

The rules cover the scope, meaning which systems may be tested, and the dates and times. They state which methods are allowed or banned, such as tricking staff or overloading systems. They name emergency contacts, and they say how any data that is found will be handled. If a tester causes an outage or finds signs of a real attacker, the tester stops and calls the named contact.

Box types describe what the tester knows at the start. Learn them as a set.

- White box: full knowledge. The tester has network maps, code and details. It is also called a known environment test.
- Gray box: partial knowledge. The tester has some details, perhaps a normal user account. It is also called a partially known environment test.
- Black box: zero knowledge. The tester starts with nothing, like an outsider. It is also called an unknown environment test.

Here is an everyday picture. A locksmith testing your home might be given the floor plans and a key. That is white box. The locksmith might be given only the address and told which room is the bedroom. That is gray box. Or the locksmith might be told nothing but the street name. That is black box.

Each has a purpose. White box covers the most ground in the available time. Gray box is a good copy of an insider, or of an attacker who has stolen a login. Black box is the most realistic copy of an outsider, but it spends much of its time simply finding things out, and it may miss a lot.

A different question is what the defenders know. In a blind test, the tester has only public information, but the defenders know that a test is coming. In a double-blind test, the defenders are not told either, so their real response can be measured. In a targeted test, both sides work openly together.

Here is your takeaway. Written approval comes first, and box color tells you only how much the tester knows.

studyNotes.heading: Red, blue, purple and white teams
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at exercises that use teams, and what each color means. The outline names red, blue and purple teams directly.

A red team acts as the attacker. It copies the methods of real criminals, often over a longer period and with a specific goal, such as reaching a particular database.

A blue team defends and responds. It watches the systems, detects the attack and shuts it down.

A purple team is red and blue working together and sharing what they learn. The attacker shows a technique, the defender checks whether it was seen, and together they improve the detection on the spot.

Think about a football team. In a practice match, some players act as the opposing attack. That is the red team. The defenders try to stop them. That is the blue team. Afterwards, the two groups watch the video together and work out why a goal was scored. That is purple.

One more color causes confusion. A white team acts as the referee in an exercise. It sets the rules, watches both sides and judges the results. Do not mix up a white team with a white box test. A white box test describes how much the tester knows. A white team describes a role.

How is a red team different from an ordinary penetration test? A penetration test usually tries to find as many weaknesses as possible within a fixed scope. A red team usually has a goal, and it tries to reach that goal quietly. It tests the people and the processes of the defense as much as it tests the technology.

Here is a workplace example. A bank's red team spends a month trying to reach a payments server without being noticed. It succeeds through a fake email, and the blue team never sees it. If the two teams never talk, the bank learns only that it failed. So they run a purple session. The red team replays each step, the blue team finds out which alert was missing, and that alert is added and tested.

The manager's view is simple. An exercise that ends with a scoreboard is worth less than one that ends with better defenses.

Here is what to take away. Red attacks, blue defends, purple shares the learning and white referees.

keyTerms.meaning: A weakness that could be used to cause harm.
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: a public list that gives each known flaw a unique name.
Common Vulnerability Scoring System: a severity score from 0.0 to 10.0.
A scan that logs in, so it can see deeper and give more accurate results.
A tool reports a problem that is not real.
A tool misses a problem that is real.
An approved attempt to break in, to prove what an attacker could do.
The written, approved limits of a test.
A test where the tester starts with zero knowledge of the target.
Attackers and defenders working together and sharing what they learn.

keyPoints: A vulnerability assessment finds weaknesses, and a penetration test uses them.
Written senior management approval must come before any penetration test.
CVE names a flaw, and CVSS scores it.
Credentialed scans see more and are more accurate.
NIST phases in order are planning, discovery, attack and reporting.
topics.memoryHook: Scan finds the open window. Pen test climbs through it. Permission comes before both.

question.prompt: A bank has hired a firm to run a penetration test next week. The IT director gave spoken agreement in a meeting. The firm has its tools ready. What is the MOST important item to have in place before the test starts?
options: Written senior management approval with agreed rules of engagement
A complete list of the passwords that are used by all of the bank's administrators
A fresh vulnerability scan of every server, completed within the past seven days
An agreement that the bank's security team will not be told anything about the test
question.explanation: Written approval and rules of engagement make the test legal and set its limits. A recent scan is useful, and it is the tempting choice, but it does not give permission. Without proper permission, testing can be a crime.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A newly announced software flaw has a Common Vulnerability Scoring System score of 6.9. Which severity band does this score fall into?
options: Low
High
Medium
Critical
practiceQuestions.explanation: Medium runs from 4.0 to 6.9, so 6.9 is at the very top of Medium. High is tempting because the score is so close, but High begins at 7.0.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A manager sees the label CVE-2024-1234 on a report, with the figure 9.8 beside it. Which statement BEST describes these two items?
options: The label gives the severity of the flaw, and the figure gives its unique name
The label is the flaw's unique name, and the figure is its CVSS severity score
Both of the items show how many systems in the company have been affected
Both of the items are private references created by the scanning tool's vendor
practiceQuestions.explanation: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures gives a flaw its unique name, and the Common Vulnerability Scoring System gives its severity. The first option is the classic mix-up, with the two roles reversed.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A penetration tester breaks into a web server and, from that server, can now see an internal network that was not visible before. Following the four phases in NIST Special Publication 800-115, what happens NEXT?
options: The tester goes back to discovery to examine the newly visible systems
The tester stops work and returns to the planning phase to begin the test again
The tester moves straight to the final report, because the break-in has succeeded
The tester deletes all of the server's logs to remain hidden during the test
practiceQuestions.explanation: The attack phase feeds back into discovery when new systems come into view, as long as they are in scope. Going straight to the report is tempting, but the test is not finished and more can be learned.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A firm has agreed the goals of a penetration test with a client, and senior management has signed the approval and the rules of engagement. Which phase comes NEXT in the NIST four-phase method?
options: Reporting
Attack
Remediation
Discovery
practiceQuestions.explanation: The order is planning, discovery, attack and reporting, so discovery follows planning. Attack is tempting, but the tester must first gather information about the target.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company wants a test that copies an attacker who has stolen one ordinary employee's login. The testers will be given that login and nothing else. What type of test is this?
options: White box
Black box
Gray box
Double-blind
practiceQuestions.explanation: Gray box means partial knowledge, such as a normal user account. Black box is tempting because the testers know little, but black box means they start with nothing at all.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company has only three days of testing budget for a complex application. It wants the most flaws found in that time and is willing to hand over its source code and network diagrams. Which approach is BEST?
options: White box
Black box
Gray box
Blind
practiceQuestions.explanation: With full knowledge, testers spend their time finding flaws and not learning the target. Black box is tempting because it is realistic, but much of three days would be spent on reconnaissance.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An organization's attackers and defenders complete separate exercises and hand in separate reports. Detection has not improved in two years. What should the security manager do?
options: Hire a second attacking team to increase the pressure on the defenders
Run purple team exercises
Keep the attackers' methods secret from the defenders for a further year
Reduce the exercises to once every two years in order to save money
practiceQuestions.explanation: A purple team approach has the attackers and defenders share techniques and improve detection together. Another attacking team is tempting, but it adds more findings without fixing the failure to share them.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security manager wants the most accurate picture of the missing patches, meaning software fixes, on 400 company servers. Which approach BEST meets this need?
options: An uncredentialed scan from the public internet
A network discovery scan of all company ports
A black box penetration test of the servers
A credentialed vulnerability scan
practiceQuestions.explanation: A credentialed scan logs in and can see installed software and missing patches directly. A black box test is tempting because it sounds thorough, but it only looks at what can be reached and would not list all missing patches.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A monthly scan reported a server as clean. A week later, attackers used a flaw on that server that had been public for a year and was present at the time of the scan. What did the scan produce?
options: A false negative
A true negative
A false positive
A true positive
practiceQuestions.explanation: A false negative misses a problem that really exists. False positive is tempting because the words sound similar, but a false positive reports a problem that does not exist.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company's leaders want to measure how its defenders really respond to an attack. The testers will have only public information. Which type of test BEST meets this goal?
options: A targeted test run openly by both sides
A blind test that the defenders have been told about
A double-blind test
A white box test using the company's own full network diagrams
practiceQuestions.explanation: In a double-blind test, the defenders are not told about the test, so their real response is measured. A blind test is tempting, but the defenders know it is coming and so may behave differently.

topics.name: Other security control tests
topics.simpleExplanation: Scans and break-in tests are not the only checks. Think of a shop. The owner reads the alarm records. A staff member makes a pretend purchase to see that the till works. Someone reads the rule book for mistakes. Someone else asks how a dishonest customer might cheat. The owner also compares the shop with the fire code. Security teams use the same kinds of checks on their controls, which are the safeguards that reduce risk. Each check finds problems that others miss.

studyNotes.heading: Log reviews
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we will look at log reviews, which are one of the oldest and most useful ways of checking whether controls are working. A control is a safeguard that reduces risk.

A log is a record of events, such as a failed sign-in or a changed file. A log review looks through those records for signs of trouble or misuse.

Think about the visitors' book at the front desk of an office. On its own, it does nothing. But if someone reads it, they may notice that the same stranger has signed in every night at midnight.

Four things make log reviews work well.

First, synchronize all the clocks, often with Network Time Protocol, or NTP. That is the standard way for computers to agree on the time. If one server's clock is six minutes fast, you cannot put events in the right order, and your timeline may not be trusted in court.

Second, protect the logs from being changed or deleted. An attacker often tries to erase their tracks. Sending logs quickly to a separate, protected system makes this far harder, and it also means that administrators cannot quietly alter records of their own actions.

Third, collect logs centrally. A Security Information and Event Management tool, or SIEM, gathers logs from many systems, links related events and raises alerts.

Fourth, keep logs for as long as policy and law require, and no longer than necessary.

There is far too much data for anyone to read every line, so organizations filter it. A clipping level is a set limit below which events are ignored. For example, one failed sign-in is normal, so an alert is raised only after five failures in a short time. Clipping saves effort, but set it too high and real attacks will slip past.

Here is a workplace example. A bank's SIEM alerts on fifty failed sign-ins against one account, followed by a success, all from another country. Because the clocks agree across systems, the analyst can follow the attacker from the sign-in to the database within minutes.

Reviews must also be done regularly and acted upon. Logs that nobody reads are only a storage bill.

Here is your takeaway. Useful logs need synchronized clocks, protection, central collection, sensible filtering and someone who really reads the results.

studyNotes.heading: Synthetic transactions, real user monitoring and benchmarks
studyNotes.body:
Next, we will look at two ways of watching a running service, and at how benchmarks are used. The exam likes to compare the first two.

A synthetic transaction is a scripted, pretend action with a known correct result. A script carries out the same steps over and over and checks the answer. Because it does not depend on people, it is active monitoring. It generates its own traffic.

Real user monitoring is different. It passively watches what real people actually do, and records their real experience. It adds no test traffic of its own, but it needs real users.

Think about a restaurant owner. Sending a pretend customer to order the same meal every day, and timing it, is a synthetic transaction. It works even on a quiet Tuesday. Watching the real customers in a busy dining room, and noticing who waits too long, is real user monitoring. It shows real experience, but on a day with no customers there is nothing to see.

Here are the differences that matter. Synthetic transactions are active, scheduled and repeatable. They can run at night, and they can catch a failure before any customer does. But they only test the paths that were scripted.

Real user monitoring is passive, and it reflects real devices, real locations and real behavior. But it needs traffic, and it tells you about a problem only after real people have met it.

Here is a workplace example. An online shop runs a script that buys a test item every ten minutes from three countries. At three in the morning, the script fails, and staff are alerted before the morning rush. The shop's real user monitoring separately shows that customers using older phones in one region are getting slow pages. The script had never tried that path. The two methods work well together.

A benchmark compares a system with a fixed reference. That reference might be a past level of performance, which is often called a baseline. Or it might be a secure settings guide, such as those from the Center for Internet Security, or CIS. If a server is compared with the CIS guide, every difference can be reviewed.

Here is what to take away. Synthetic is scripted and active and needs no users. Real user monitoring is passive and needs real people. A benchmark compares against a known reference.

studyNotes.heading: Code review and code testing
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at how software itself is checked, both by reading it and by running it.

Code review means reading program code to find flaws. Think about having a friend proofread an important letter. A fresh pair of eyes catches what the writer no longer sees. Reviews can be informal, as when one developer looks at another's change.

The most formal method is a Fagan inspection, which has six steps, in this order.

- Planning
- Overview
- Preparation
- Inspection
- Rework
- Follow-up

In planning, the team decides what will be reviewed and who will attend. The overview introduces the code to the team. In preparation, each reviewer studies the code alone. In the inspection meeting, the team finds and records the defects. In rework, the author fixes them. In follow-up, someone confirms that the fixes were really made. Notice that finding the defects and fixing them are separate steps.

There are also two main kinds of tool-based testing.

Static testing, or Static Application Security Testing, known as SAST, checks code that is not running. It reads the source code, and it can find problems early, before the program can even be used.

Dynamic testing, or Dynamic Application Security Testing, known as DAST, checks the program while it runs. It behaves like a user sending requests, and it can find problems that only appear at run time, such as a poor server setting.

Think of a new recipe. Static testing is reading the recipe and spotting that it asks for a whole cup of salt. Dynamic testing is cooking the dish and tasting it. You need both.

Fuzz testing sends unexpected or random input to a running program to find crashes and flaws. It comes in two kinds. Mutation fuzzing changes real input, for example by flipping parts of a valid file. Generation fuzzing builds new input from knowledge of the expected format, so it can go deeper.

Here is a workplace example. A payments team runs static testing on each code change, and holds a formal inspection for the code that moves money. It then uses dynamic testing and fuzz testing on the running test system. Each method finds things the others miss.

Here is your takeaway. Know the six Fagan steps in order. Static testing needs no running code, while dynamic and fuzz testing do.

studyNotes.heading: Misuse cases and test coverage
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at how to test for abuse, and how to measure how much of a program was really tested.

A use case describes normal use of a system. A misuse case, sometimes called an abuse case, describes how someone might deliberately or carelessly abuse it. Most ordinary tests check that a program does what it should. Misuse case testing checks that it refuses to do what it should not.

Think about a vending machine. The normal use is to put in a coin and receive a drink. A misuse case asks other questions. What if someone uses a fake coin? What if someone presses every button at once? What if someone pulls the coin back on a string?

Here is a workplace example. An online shop's normal use case is that a customer enters a quantity of two and pays. A misuse case asks whether a customer can enter a quantity of minus five and receive a refund. Another asks whether a customer can change the price in the web page before paying. A test is written for each of these. The best misuse cases come from thinking like an attacker, and they are best written during design, when problems are cheapest to fix.

Test coverage analysis shows how much of a program or of its requirements was tested. Coverage is the number of items tested, divided by the total number of items, times 100, and the answer is a percentage.

Let us work one through. A program has 500 branches. A branch is a decision path in the code, such as the yes or no of an if statement. The tests reach 450 of them. So 450 divided by 500 is 0.9, and 0.9 times 100 is 90 percent.

Coverage can be measured in several ways, and you should recognize this set.

- Branch coverage: has every decision path been taken?
- Condition coverage: has each logical condition been tried in each possible way?
- Function coverage: has every function been called?
- Loop coverage: has every loop been run in the ways it could be?
- Statement coverage: has every line of code been run?

Be careful. High coverage shows what was tested. It does not prove the code is secure.

Here is what to take away. Misuse cases test for abuse, and coverage measures how much was tested but never how good it is.

studyNotes.heading: Interface testing
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at interface testing, because flaws often hide in the places where two things connect.

An interface is a point where two things meet and exchange information. Think about the counter at a bank. It is where the customer and the bank's systems meet. A teller who checks each form carefully is one thing. A teller who accepts anything is the weak point of the whole bank, however strong the vault may be.

The outline names three interfaces, and you should know the set.

- User interface: the screens and buttons that people use.
- Network interface: the connections between systems.
- Application Programming Interface, or API: the way that programs ask each other for data or services.

Testing a user interface means trying what a person might try. Does a field reject bad entries? Does the page hide things it should? Remember that what a screen hides, a determined person can still ask for directly, so checks must also be made on the server side.

Testing a network interface means looking at how systems connect. Are the connections encrypted, which means scrambled so outsiders cannot read them? Are only the expected services reachable?

Testing an API means sending requests directly to it, without using the normal screens. Check that it confirms who is calling, which is called authentication. Then check that it limits what that caller may do, which is called authorization. Also check that it limits how many requests a caller can send.

For all three interfaces, try good input, bad input and boundary values. A boundary value is one at the very edge of what is allowed. If a field allows ages 18 to 65, try 17, 18, 65 and 66. Errors often live right at the edges.

Here is a workplace example. A mobile banking application shows each customer only that customer's own statements. A tester sends a request straight to the API and changes the account number in it. If the API returns another customer's statement, there is a serious flaw, even though the screens looked perfectly safe.

Also check that a failure leaves the system in a safe state, and that error messages give away nothing useful.

Here is your takeaway. Test user, network and application programming interfaces with good, bad and boundary input, and always check who is calling.

studyNotes.heading: Breach attack simulation and compliance checks
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at two more checks: one that keeps testing defenses all the time, and one that compares what you do with what you are required to do.

Breach attack simulation tools run safe, automated copies of real attack methods. They run often, sometimes continuously, and they show whether your defenses block or detect each one.

Think about a fire drill. A real fire tells you how good your plan was, but too late. A drill, repeated regularly, shows whether the alarm still sounds and whether people still know where to go, and nobody gets hurt.

How is this different from the other kinds of test? A vulnerability scan looks for weaknesses and lists them. A penetration test uses human creativity to break in, and it happens only now and then. A breach attack simulation is automated and repeated, and it tests whether your existing controls still respond to known attack methods. It will not invent a clever new attack, but it will notice when a control has quietly stopped working.

Here is a workplace example. A company's simulation tool safely copies the steps of a well-known ransomware attack every week. Ransomware is harmful software that locks files and demands payment. For months, the alerts fire correctly. Then a change to one system turns off a detection rule. The next weekly run shows the gap, and it is fixed the same day. A yearly penetration test might not have caught that for eleven months.

A compliance check compares controls with a requirement, such as a law, a contract or a policy. One example is the Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard, or PCI DSS, which covers card payments.

Compliance checks answer a narrow question: do we do what the requirement says? That is important, but it is not the same as being safe. A company can pass a check on Friday and be breached on Saturday, through a risk the standard never addressed. Remember that compliant does not always mean secure.

A manager uses both. Compliance is the minimum that the law or contract demands. Risk management decides what else is needed.

Here is what to take away. Breach attack simulation repeatedly proves that defenses still respond, and a compliance check shows that requirements are met but never proves that you are secure.

A set limit below which events are not reported.
A scripted, pretend action with a known correct result.
Passively watching the actions of real users.
A formal, six-step code review.
Sending unexpected or random input to find crashes and flaws.
A description of how someone might abuse a system.
The share of a program or its requirements that was tested.
Application Programming Interface: the way programs ask each other for data.
Automated, safe, repeated copies of real attacks that show whether defenses work.

Synthetic transactions are active, and real user monitoring is passive.
Static testing needs no running code, but dynamic testing does.
Coverage equals items tested divided by total items, times 100.
Being compliant does not always mean being secure.
topics.memoryHook: Fagan's six: People Often Prepare In Rushed Fashion (Planning, Overview, Preparation, Inspection, Rework, Follow-up).

question.prompt: A shop's online checkout had an outage overnight, and nobody noticed until morning. Management wants to know every 15 minutes, day and night, that checkout works and how quickly it responds, even when no customers are online. Which approach BEST meets this need?
options: Real user monitoring of the checkout pages throughout the day and night
A weekly review of the web server logs by the operations team
Static testing of the checkout code each time that a new release is built
Synthetic transactions
question.explanation: Scripted test purchases run on a schedule, so they work even when the site is empty. Real user monitoring is tempting, but it needs real users. With no customers online, it has nothing to measure.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A global online retailer wants to understand how its website actually performs for its customers on different phones and in different countries. Which approach BEST meets this need?
options: Synthetic transactions run from the head office
Real user monitoring
Static testing of the website's source code
A benchmark of the servers against a secure settings guide
practiceQuestions.explanation: Real user monitoring passively records the experience of real customers on their real devices. Synthetic transactions are tempting, but a script from one place only follows the paths that were written for it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Investigators cannot work out the order of events during an incident, because the logs from different servers appear to disagree by several minutes. What would have BEST prevented this problem?
options: Keeping the logs on each server for a much longer period of time
Lowering the clipping level so that more events are recorded
Encrypting all of the logs before they leave each server
Synchronizing all clocks with Network Time Protocol
practiceQuestions.explanation: Agreed time across systems is what allows events to be placed in order. Keeping logs for longer is useful, but older logs with wrong times would still disagree.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A security analyst receives thousands of alerts each day because every single failed sign-in raises one. Most are simple typing errors. Which change would BEST reduce the noise while still catching repeated attempts?
options: Set a clipping level
Stop collecting sign-in events on all of the company's systems
Require staff to report each of their own typing errors to the help desk
Review the sign-in logs once a year instead of each day
practiceQuestions.explanation: A clipping level ignores events below a set limit, so one mistake is ignored and repeated failures are not. Stopping the collection is tempting because it ends the noise, but it also ends the detection.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A software team is holding a Fagan inspection. The team has just finished the inspection meeting and recorded a list of defects. What is the NEXT step?
options: Follow-up
Preparation
Rework
Overview
practiceQuestions.explanation: The order is planning, overview, preparation, inspection, rework and follow-up. Follow-up is tempting, but the author must first fix the defects so that there is something to confirm.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A development team wants to find security flaws as early as possible, while the application is still being written and cannot yet be run. Which method is BEST?
options: Dynamic testing
Fuzz testing
Real user monitoring
Static testing
practiceQuestions.explanation: Static testing examines code that is not running, so it can be used before the application works. Dynamic and fuzz testing are tempting, but both need a running program.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Before an online shop launches a new refunds page, a tester writes a test to find out whether a customer could claim a refund twice for one purchase. Which kind of testing is this?
options: Misuse case testing
Synthetic transaction monitoring
Benchmark comparison
Loop coverage analysis
practiceQuestions.explanation: A misuse case describes how someone could abuse a system, and this test checks exactly that. Synthetic transactions are tempting, but they usually repeat a normal path to prove that a service works.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A program contains 1,000 statements. The test suite ran 800 of them. A project manager asks for the statement coverage. What is the correct answer?
options: 20 percent
80 percent
125 percent
800 percent
practiceQuestions.explanation: Coverage is the items tested divided by the total, times 100, so 800 divided by 1,000 times 100 is 80 percent. 20 percent is tempting, but that is the share that was not tested.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A tester sends requests straight to a mobile application's Application Programming Interface and changes the customer number in each request. The screens of the application never allow this. What is the tester MOST likely checking?
options: How fast the mobile screens load on an older model of telephone
Whether the interface limits each caller to that caller's own data
Whether the application's source code follows the agreed naming rules
How much of the mobile application's code has been covered by tests
practiceQuestions.explanation: Changing the customer number tests authorization, which means whether the API limits what a caller may reach. Checks in the screens alone are not enough, because a caller can skip the screens and go straight to the API.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A company passes its annual compliance check against a card payment standard. The chief executive says the company can now stop worrying about security for the year. What should the security manager advise?
options: Agree, because a passed check shows that all risks have been removed
Agree, but ask for a second check against the same standard
Explain that compliance is a minimum and that risks must still be managed
Explain that compliance checks are of no value and should be stopped
practiceQuestions.explanation: Compliance shows that certain requirements were met at a point in time, and it does not remove all risk. The last option is tempting to a frustrated manager, but compliance checks are needed, just not sufficient.

practiceQuestions.prompt: An organization wants to compare the settings on its new servers against a recognized secure configuration guide, and to list every difference. What is this activity called?
options: Benchmarking
Fuzz testing
Mutation testing
Penetration testing
practiceQuestions.explanation: A benchmark compares a system with a fixed reference, such as a secure settings guide. Penetration testing is tempting because it also looks for weaknesses, but it tries to break in instead of comparing settings.

topics.name: Collecting security process data
topics.simpleExplanation: A school can have good fire doors and still be unsafe if nobody runs fire drills. So the principal keeps records. Who attended? How long did it take? Did anything go wrong? Security needs the same kind of records. Companies collect data about accounts, management approvals, backups, staff training and recovery tests. This data shows whether daily security work is really happening. Managers use the numbers to see how well things went and where danger is growing, so they can act early.

studyNotes.heading: What process data is
studyNotes.body:
In this first part, we will look at what security process data is, and why a security program needs it.

Process data is the record that security activities are happening as they should. Technical tests check machines. Process data checks routines and people. The exam outline says this data can be technical or administrative. Technical data comes from systems, such as the result of a backup job. Administrative data comes from business activity, such as a signed approval or a training record.

Think about a school that has excellent fire doors and a sensible fire plan. Are the drills really happening? How long did the last one take? Was anyone missing? Without those records, the principal is only hoping. The records are what turn hope into knowledge.

The outline names several areas, and you should know the set.

- Account management
- Management review and approval
- Management reporting and metrics, including key performance and risk indicators
- Backup verification data
- Training and awareness
- Disaster recovery and business continuity

We will take each of these in turn in this topic.

A metric is simply a number that measures something. Good process data has a few qualities. It must be accurate, so that people can trust it. It must be complete, so that it does not hide the awkward cases. It must be collected regularly and in the same way each time, so that one month can be compared with the next. And it must help someone make a decision. A number that nobody uses is only a cost.

Here is a workplace example. A company reports each month that 99 percent of its laptops are protected. A closer look shows that the figure only counts laptops already registered in the management tool. Laptops bought by departments on their own are never counted. The number looked excellent, but it was incomplete, and it hid the real risk.

Think like a manager here. Before you trust a number, ask where it came from, what it leaves out and what decision it supports. Also protect the data, because it can reveal exactly where the organization is weak.

Here is your takeaway. Process data proves that security routines are really happening, and it is only useful if it is accurate, complete, consistent and used for decisions.

studyNotes.heading: Account management
studyNotes.body:
Next, we will look at account management, which means checking who has access to what, and whether they still should.

Every account should belong to a real person with a real need. Think about the keys to an apartment building. New tenants get a key to their own flat. A tenant who moves upstairs should give back the old key. A tenant who leaves should hand in every key. Keys that nobody can account for are a danger to everyone in the building.

There are four groups to check.

Joiners, who are new staff, should get only the access that has been approved.

Movers, who change jobs inside the company, should lose the access they no longer need. If they do not, access builds up over time. That is called privilege creep.

Leavers, who have departed, should be disabled quickly.

Privileged accounts have powerful rights, such as those of system administrators. These should be few in number, closely watched and reviewed more often than the others.

Good data for this area includes the number of accounts with no clear owner, how long it takes to disable a leaver's account, and how many access reviews were finished on time.

A particular word to know is recertification, or attestation. It means that a manager regularly confirms that each person on the team still needs the access they have.

Now here is a worked example, step by step. A company wants to test whether its leaver process works.

First, it takes a sample of 200 accounts.

Second, it compares them with the staff list held by human resources.

Third, it finds that 6 of the accounts belong to people who have left.

Fourth, it calculates the failure rate. That is 6 divided by 200, which is 0.03. And 0.03 times 100 is 3 percent.

Fifth, it disables those 6 accounts straight away. That deals with the symptom.

Sixth, it looks at why the accounts stayed active, and it finds that human resources never tells the technical team when somebody resigns. Linking those two steps fixes the cause.

The exam mindset here is clear. Deleting the accounts is necessary, but it does not stop the same thing from happening next quarter. Always fix the process.

Here is what to take away. Check joiners, movers, leavers and privileged accounts, and when you find a failure, fix the process behind it.

studyNotes.heading: Management review and approval
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at management review and approval, and at how results are reported upward.

Managers must look at security results, decide what to do and record that decision. This shows oversight, which means that someone responsible is really watching.

Think about a parent signing a child's school report. If the parent signs without reading it, the signature is worthless. If the parent reads it, talks about the poor math grade and arranges help, the signature means something. Security approvals work in the same way. A signature given without reading adds no value.

Managers review policies, access requests, test results, changes to systems and accepted risks. The record of each review should show who reviewed it, when, what they decided and why.

Two rules protect the quality of an approval. First, the approver needs real authority, which means the power to make that decision for the business. Second, the approver should not be the person who made the request. This is separation of duties, which means that no one person controls a whole task. If an engineer could request and approve their own access, the approval would prove nothing.

There is also a formal management review in many standards. ISO 27001, an international standard for managing information security, requires top management to review its security management system at planned intervals. ISO stands for the International Organization for Standardization.

Management reporting and metrics are how the results get to those managers. Good reporting is written for its reader. Senior leaders do not need a list of 4,000 scanner findings. They need to know whether risk is going up or down, whether targets are being met and what decisions they must make.

Here is a workplace example. A security manager's monthly report once listed dozens of technical figures, and nobody on the executive team read it. The manager replaced it with a single page showing five measures, the target for each, the trend over six months and the one decision required this month. Executives began to ask questions and to approve funding.

From the exam's point of view, a manager's review is itself a piece of evidence. An auditor may ask to see the record that a review took place.

Here is your takeaway. Reviews must be real, recorded and done by someone with authority who is independent of the request, and reports must be written for their reader.

studyNotes.heading: KPIs and KRIs
studyNotes.body:
Now we will look at two measures that are easy to confuse: key performance indicators and key risk indicators. The difference is direction.

A Key Performance Indicator, or KPI, looks back. It asks: how well did we do? A Key Risk Indicator, or KRI, looks ahead. It is an early warning. It asks: is danger growing?

Think about driving a car. The rear-view mirror shows the road you have already covered. The headlights show what is coming. A KPI is the mirror, and a KRI is the headlights. Or think about your health. Having run three times last week is a performance measure. A blood pressure reading that is creeping up is a warning about what may happen later.

Let us work through an example. A patch is a software fix.

Here is a KPI. In one month, 950 of 1,000 computers were patched on time. That is 950 divided by 1,000, which is 0.95. And 0.95 times 100 is 95 percent. The target was 98 percent, so the team missed the target by 3 percentage points.

Here is a KRI. The number of unpatched servers facing the internet rose from 2 to 9 in three months. Nothing bad has happened yet, but the risk is growing, and it should raise a flag.

Other common KPIs are the percentage of incidents closed on time, the mean time to detect an incident, and the mean time to respond to one. Mean simply means the average. Other common KRIs are a rising number of privileged accounts, more systems that are no longer supported by their vendor, and more overdue audit findings.

A useful test is to ask what the number tells you to do. If it reports a finished result, it is probably a KPI. If it warns you to act before harm happens, it is probably a KRI. The same raw figure can sometimes serve as either one, depending on how it is used, so look carefully at what the scenario is asking.

A good measure links to a business goal, is measured the same way each time, has a target or threshold and makes sense to its reader. A threshold is the level at which someone must take action.

Here is what to take away. A KPI tells you how you did, and a KRI warns you where risk is heading.

studyNotes.heading: Backups, training and awareness
studyNotes.body:
In this part, we will look at two more kinds of evidence: proof that backups work, and proof that people are learning.

A backup is a copy of data that is kept so that it can be restored. A backup log shows that a job ran. Only a test restore proves that data can be recovered.

Think about a spare tire in the trunk of your car. Having one is reassuring. But if it has gone flat, or the jack is missing, you only find out at the side of the road. The sensible thing is to check it before you need it.

Useful backup verification data includes job success or failure, the results of test restores, the time that each restore took and the location of offsite copies. A common guideline is three copies of your data, on two different kinds of storage, with one copy offsite. Copies that cannot be altered are also valuable, because ransomware, which is software that locks files and demands payment, often attacks backups first.

Here is a workplace example. A company's backup report has shown success every day for a year. In a test restore, the files come back, but one database is damaged, and the whole restore takes nine hours. The business had assumed two hours. The report was accurate, but it did not answer the question that mattered.

Now let us turn to people. There are three levels of learning, and the exam may test them as a set.

- Awareness: helps people notice danger. It answers the question what.
- Training: teaches a skill for a job. It answers the question how.
- Education: builds deep understanding. It answers the question why.

Useful data includes course completion, how many staff click on test phishing emails and how many report them. Phishing means tricking people through false messages.

Let us work one through. A company sends a test phishing email to 1,000 staff, and 120 click. That is 120 divided by 1,000, times 100, which is 12 percent. Six months after training, only 60 click. That is 6 percent. Reports of suspicious emails also go up. This is a real improvement in behavior.

Completion alone proves only that people attended. Trends over time matter more than one result.

Here is your takeaway. Backups are proven by restoring them, and training is proven by changed behavior.

studyNotes.heading: Disaster recovery and business continuity
studyNotes.body:
In this final part, we will look at the data that shows whether an organization can survive a serious event.

Disaster recovery, or DR, brings technology back after a serious event. Business continuity, or BC, keeps important work going during and after that event. People's safety always comes first, ahead of any system or any data.

Think about a family whose kitchen is damaged by a fire. Getting everyone out safely comes first. Eating at a relative's home for a few weeks is continuity. Rebuilding the kitchen is recovery.

The data to collect includes test dates, plan review dates, recovery times achieved, problems found and lessons learned, and whether those lessons were acted upon. A plan with no recent test is only a theory.

Plan tests run from the least to the most disruptive. You should know this order exactly.

- Read-through, also called a checklist test: people read the plan and check that it is correct.
- Structured walk-through, also called a tabletop test: the team talks through a scenario together around a table.
- Simulation: people act out their response to a pretend event, without moving real work.
- Parallel: systems are brought up at the recovery site while the main site keeps running.
- Full interruption: the main site is really shut down and work moves to the recovery site.
